lead: A page replacement algorithm decides which page to throw out when a page fault occurs and no frame is free. The choice is invisible until the next fault, but over a run it changes the fault count. This chapter counts faults for the same reference string under FIFO, LRU and optimal replacement, explains Belady's anomaly, and shows why exact LRU needs hardware help. The same ideas run in every demand-paged system, from a phone opening apps to a server under memory pressure.
prereq: You need: 4.7 for page faults and 4.4 for frames and page-table entries.

blocks.text: A reference string is the ordered list of page numbers a process asks for. Use 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. A frame is one physical page slot. The OS starts with all frames empty. If the requested page is already in a frame, that reference is a hit: no disk read and no replacement. If it is not, the reference is a fault: the OS loads the page. A free frame is used if one exists. When every frame is full, the OS must pick a victim page, write it back if it is dirty, and load the new page into that frame. The choice of victim is the page replacement algorithm.

Count faults by walking the string left to right and recording the frames after each reference. Mark H for a hit and F for a fault. The same string must be used for every algorithm, otherwise the counts cannot be compared.

blocks.where: faults is the number of F marks; references is the number of page requests in the string. For the string above there are 12 references, so FIFO's 9 faults give 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75.

blocks.text: FIFO keeps pages in a queue in arrival order. A new page joins the tail. When a victim is needed, the head page is evicted: it is the page that arrived first. With three frames and the string above, references 1, 2, 3 and 4 give four faults and evict 1. The frames become 2, 3, 4. Reference 1 then faults and evicts 2; reference 2 faults and evicts 3; reference 5 faults and evicts 4. References 1 and 2 now hit. Reference 3 faults and evicts 1; reference 4 faults and evicts 2; reference 5 hits. Total = 9 faults.

FIFO has Belady's anomaly: more frames can cause more faults. The same string under FIFO with four frames gives 10 faults, one more than with three frames. Extra frames change the eviction order, and the new order happens to miss more often. LRU and OPT do not show this anomaly; they are stack algorithms, so adding frames cannot increase their fault count.

LRU evicts the page whose last use is farthest in the past. One exact implementation keeps a stack: every reference moves that page to the top, and the bottom page is the victim. Another uses a counter in each page-table entry: a global clock is incremented on every memory access, the page's counter is set to the clock value, and the smallest counter is evicted. Aging approximates this with a shift register: the hardware sets a reference bit, the OS shifts it into the register periodically, and the smallest register value is evicted.

Exact LRU needs hardware help because a stack or counter must be updated on every memory access; doing that in software would double the cost of each access. Second-chance is a cheap approximation: it is FIFO plus a reference bit. If the oldest page has bit 0, evict it; if bit 1, clear the bit and move it to the back of the queue. Clock does the same with frames in a circle and a moving hand.

OPT (optimal, or MIN) evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future; a page never used again is evicted first. It needs the future reference string, so it cannot run online. It is a benchmark: no real algorithm can beat it. On the same string, FIFO = 9, LRU = 10, OPT = 7. LRU is worse than FIFO here, which shows that no simple algorithm wins on every string. LFU evicts the least frequently used page and MFU the most frequently used; only a few universities teach them, because counts age badly and need extra fields.

examples.question: For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and three frames, count page faults for FIFO, LRU and OPT. Show the frame contents after each reference.
steps: Start all frames empty. Use F for fault and H for hit.

FIFO: after 1 [1] F1; after 2 [1,2] F2; after 3 [1,2,3] F3; after 4 [2,3,4] F4 (evict 1); after 1 [3,4,1] F5 (evict 2); after 2 [4,1,2] F6 (evict 3); after 5 [1,2,5] F7 (evict 4); after 1 H; after 2 H; after 3 [2,5,3] F8 (evict 1); after 4 [5,3,4] F9 (evict 2); after 5 H. FIFO faults = 9.

LRU: after 1 [1] F1; after 2 [1,2] F2; after 3 [1,2,3] F3; after 4 [2,3,4] F4 (evict 1); after 1 [3,4,1] F5 (evict 2); after 2 [4,1,2] F6 (evict 3); after 5 [1,2,5] F7 (evict 4); after 1 H; after 2 H; after 3 [1,2,3] F8 (evict 5); after 4 [2,3,4] F9 (evict 1); after 5 [3,4,5] F10 (evict 2). LRU faults = 10.

OPT: after 1 [1] F1; after 2 [1,2] F2; after 3 [1,2,3] F3; after 4 [1,2,4] F4 (evict 3; next uses: 1 at 5, 2 at 6, 3 at 10); after 1 H; after 2 H; after 5 [1,2,5] F5 (evict 4; next use 4 at 11); after 1 H; after 2 H; after 3 [2,5,3] F6 (evict 1; 1 never used again); after 4 [5,3,4] F7 (evict 2; 2 never used again); after 5 H. OPT faults = 7.
examples.answer: FIFO = 9 faults, LRU = 10 faults, OPT = 7 faults.

traps: FIFO is not LRU: FIFO evicts the page loaded first, while LRU evicts the page used least recently. A page loaded long ago but used recently is kept by LRU and evicted by FIFO.
Do not count a hit as a fault. The fault count is the number of F marks, not the number of references.
Belady's anomaly is a FIFO example, not a rule for every algorithm. More frames can increase FIFO faults, but not LRU or OPT faults.
OPT is not implementable online; it needs future page references. Use it only as a lower bound for comparing real algorithms.
Exact LRU needs a hardware-maintained stack or time counter. A software-only stack on every memory access is too slow.

quiz.q: Define reference string and page fault.
quiz.a: A reference string is the ordered list of page numbers a process asks for. A page fault is the event when the requested page is not in any frame, so the OS must load it.

quiz.q: Why can FIFO suffer Belady's anomaly while LRU cannot?
quiz.a: FIFO is not a stack algorithm: adding frames can change which page is oldest at each eviction and increase misses. LRU is a stack algorithm: the set of pages kept with n frames is always a subset of the set kept with n+1 frames, so adding frames cannot increase faults.

quiz.q: For the string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with four frames under FIFO, count faults.
quiz.a: Frames after each reference: 1 F [1]; 2 F [1,2]; 3 F [1,2,3]; 4 F [1,2,3,4]; 1 H; 2 H; 5 F evict 1 [2,3,4,5]; 1 F evict 2 [3,4,5,1]; 2 F evict 3 [4,5,1,2]; 3 F evict 4 [5,1,2,3]; 4 F evict 5 [1,2,3,4]; 5 F evict 1 [2,3,4,5]. Total = 10 faults.

quiz.q: With three frames and string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, count faults under LRU.
quiz.a: After 1 [1] F; 2 [1,2] F; 3 [1,2,3] F; 4 evict 1 [2,3,4] F; 1 evict 2 [3,4,1] F; 2 evict 3 [4,1,2] F; 5 evict 4 [1,2,5] F. Total = 7 faults.

quiz.q: On the chapter string, LRU has 10 faults and FIFO has 9. What does this say about always using LRU?
quiz.a: No replacement algorithm is best on every string. LRU can be worse than FIFO for a particular access pattern, even though LRU usually has better locality behaviour. OPT gives the lower bound, and real systems use approximations such as clock because exact LRU is costly.

quiz.q: What does the reference bit do in the second-chance algorithm?
quiz.a: Hardware sets the reference bit to 1 when a page is used. Second-chance checks the oldest page: if its bit is 0, it is evicted; if it is 1, the bit is cleared and the page is moved to the back of the queue, giving it a second chance.

quiz.q: What is OPT and why is it not used in a real OS?
quiz.a: OPT, also called MIN, evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future. It needs the future reference string, which a real OS cannot know, so it is used only as a benchmark.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real kernels use variants of clock, not exact LRU: Linux keeps active and inactive page lists and moves pages between them, while Windows uses a working-set-like clock. Search for clock page replacement, second-chance algorithm, Linux page reclaim, and Belady anomaly. The same counting method—reference string, frames, fault marks—is how you test any new policy.
